Anne Hutchinson
an HUTCH-in-son
proper noun (a colonial figure, 1591–1643)
From Anne Hutchinson (1591–1643), an Englishwoman of the Massachusetts Bay Colony whose teaching sparked the Antinomian Controversy of 1636–1638; “Anne” from the Hebrew Hannah (grace).

Biblical Definition

Anne Hutchinson was an Englishwoman of the Massachusetts Bay Colony whose teaching provoked the Antinomian Controversy of 1636–1638. A woman of evident gifts, sharp mind, and genuine zeal for free grace, she gathered hearers in her home to discuss the sermons and pressed the doctrine of grace against any reliance on works. The dictionary honours what is honourable in her: her earnest love of grace, her recoil from a religion of mere outward duty, and her courage. Yet it must name plainly the errors that the colony's synod and court condemned. She charged most of the ministers with preaching a “covenant of works” rather than a covenant of grace, drifting into antinomianism—the error that so exalts grace as to make the moral law and the fruits of sanctification needless evidence of a true work, when Scripture says faith without works is dead and that by their fruits ye shall know them. More gravely, she claimed direct, immediate revelations of the Spirit apart from and above the written Word, expecting personal voices and impressions to guide her. The dictionary marks this as a breach of two settled truths: cessationism, that the gift of new prophetic revelation ceased with the apostles, and the closed canon, the faith once for all delivered unto the saints, to which nothing is to be added. She also taught and exhorted men publicly in matters of doctrine, against the apostolic order that a woman is not to teach nor usurp authority over the man in the church. The dictionary thus honours her zeal for grace while naming her antinomianism, her claim to private revelation, and her overstepping of the complementarian order as the errors that justly drew the censure of the godly fathers of New England.

Webster 1828 Definition

The colonial figure (1591–1643) at the centre of the Antinomian Controversy in Massachusetts Bay; honoured for zeal for free grace, but named for antinomianism, claims to immediate private revelation against the closed canon, and overstepping the church's order.

ANNE HUTCHINSON, proper noun. [“Anne,” from Hebrew Hannah, grace.] An Englishwoman of Massachusetts Bay (1591–1643).

Central to the Antinomian Controversy of 1636–1638.

Honoured for her zeal for free grace against mere outward duty.

Named for antinomianism and claims of immediate private revelation.

Censured for teaching that contravened the church's order (1 Timothy 2:12).

Key Scripture

Jude 1:3 — "Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

Jas 2:17 — "Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone."

1 Ti 2:12 — "But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence."

Mt 7:20 — "Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them."

Modern Corruption

Anne Hutchinson's antinomianism slighted the law and the fruits of sanctification, her claim to immediate revelation breached cessationism and the closed canon, and her public teaching overstepped the church's order.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary honours what is honourable in Anne Hutchinson: a genuine love of free grace, a recoil from a religion of mere outward duty, and real courage. But the principle to recover is the balance her zeal upset. Her antinomianism so exalted grace as to slight the moral law and the necessary fruits of sanctification, charging the ministers with a covenant of works for pressing holiness. Scripture answers that faith without works is dead, and that by their fruits ye shall know them. Free grace does not abolish the law as the rule of the believer's life; it writes the law upon the heart. To love grace and despise the evidences of grace is to misread the gospel she meant to defend.

Two further errors must be named. She claimed direct and immediate revelations of the Spirit—voices and impressions guiding her apart from and above the written Word. The dictionary holds cessationism, that the gift of new prophetic revelation ceased with the apostles, and the closed canon, the faith once for all delivered unto the saints, to which nothing may be added. A spirit that speaks beside the Word is to be tried by the Word and, where it adds to it, refused. And she taught and exhorted men publicly in doctrine, against the apostolic order that a woman is not to teach nor usurp authority over the man in the church. The complementarian order is no slight upon her gifts but the Lord's appointment for His house. The dictionary therefore honours her zeal for grace while naming the antinomianism, the private revelation, and the overstepping of order that justly drew the censure of New England's fathers.

Hebrew Roots

From Anne (Hebrew Hannah, grace) Hutchinson (1591–1643); the colonial figure whose teaching sparked the Antinomian Controversy in Massachusetts Bay.
